extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / discrete mathematics (relations and functions)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and standard proof techniques for equivalence relations, partitions, integers modulo n, relations between sets, and functions (including injective/surjective/bijective). Includes common examples, exercises, and methods for proving or disproving properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental criterion: every proof that a relation is an equivalence relation must verify each of the three properties. The text emphasizes using all three properties in certain proofs (e.g., Theorem 11.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class equality (Theorem 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose R is an equivalence relation on a set A. Then [a] = [b] if and only if aRb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of R and basic set membership arguments to prove both directions. This result is frequently used to move between statements about representatives (aRb) and equality of classes ([a]=[b]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes form a partition (Theorem 11.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A, the set {[a]: a ∈ A} of equivalence classes forms a partition of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof requires showing (1) union of all equivalence classes equals A (every x ∈ A lies in [x]) and (2) distinct equivalence classes are disjoint (if [a] ≠ [b] then [a] ∩ [b] = ∅). Use contrapositive and Theorem 11.1 where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition of a set A is a set of non-empty subsets of A such that the union of all the subsets equals A, and the intersection of any two different subsets is ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or verifying partitions, check non-emptiness of parts, coverage of A, and pairwise disjointness. Examples illustrate how to list and reason about partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct equivalence relation from a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partition P of A, define R on A by declaring xRy iff x,y ∈ X for some X ∈ P. Then R is an equivalence relation and P is the set of equivalence classes of R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the bijection between partitions and equivalence relations: to produce an equivalence relation from a partition, check reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity derived from membership in the same block. Conversely, given an equivalence relation, its classes form a partition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting size of an equivalence relation on finite A
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is finite and equivalence classes have sizes s1, s2, ..., sk, then |R| = sum_{i=1..k} (si^2). (If every class has same size m and there are k classes with km = |A|, then |R| = k*m^2 = m*|A|.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: R contains all ordered pairs (x,y) with x and y in the same class; a class of size s contributes s^2 ordered pairs. This is the standard counting technique for equivalence relations on finite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integers modulo n: classes and Zn
rubrics_metrics.description: For n∈N, the equivalence classes of ≡ (mod n) are [0], [1], ..., [n−1]; Zn is the set of these n classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with Zn, represent elements as classes [a] and remember multiple representatives may denote the same class (e.g., [5]=[0] in Z5). Exercises include writing addition/multiplication tables and describing partitions induced by congruence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations on equivalence classes (well-definedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define [a]+[b] = [a+b] and [a]·[b] = [ab] in Zn; these operations must be well-defined (independent of choice of representatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show well-definedness by taking different representatives [a]=[a'] and [b]=[b'] and proving [ab]=[a'b'] (via divisibility by n). Typical proof uses a−a' = n k and b−b' = nℓ and expands ab − a'b' to show n divides it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation from A to B
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation from a set A to a set B is any subset R ⊆ A×B; abbreviation (x,y)∈R as xRy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When visualizing relations from A to B draw labeled nodes for each set and arrows for pairs xRy. This generalizes relations on a single set to relations between different sets (e.g., membership relation ∈).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a special relation (Definition 12.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f from A to B is a relation f ⊆ A×B such that for each a∈A, f contains exactly one ordered pair of the form (a,b). Denote (a,b)∈f as f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This set-theoretic definition removes vagueness of 'rule.' When proving something is a function, show existence and uniqueness of the pair for each input a. Visualizations: graph in AxB or arrow diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, range (Definition 12.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B, the domain is A, codomain is B, and the range is {f(a): a∈A}. The range is a subset of the codomain; the codomain is a matter of choice/context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: surjectivity depends on codomain choice. When specifying a function, explicitly state domain and codomain; equal functions must have equal domains and agree on every input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions (Definition 12.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f:A→B and g:A→D are equal iff f=g as sets, equivalently f(x)=g(x) for every x∈A (codomains may differ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that equality is pointwise equality over the domain; codomain differences do not prevent equality if values agree on domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective, surjective, bijective (Definition 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injective: for all a,a'∈A, a≠a' implies f(a)≠f(a'). Surjective: for every b∈B there exists a∈A with f(a)=b. Bijective: both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand these both logically and visually: injective = different inputs map to different outputs; surjective = every codomain element has a preimage. Note surjectivity depends on the codomain.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a function is injective
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main approaches: Direct approach (assume a≠a' and show f(a)≠f(a')) or Contrapositive approach (assume f(a)=f(a') and show a=a').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrapositive is often easier, especially when f is algebraically defined, because it begins with an equation f(a)=f(a') and manipulates it to deduce a=a'. To disprove injectivity, provide a counterexample of distinct a,a' with f(a)=f(a').

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a function is surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f:A→B is surjective: let b∈B be arbitrary and prove there exists a∈A with f(a)=b (often by solving f(a)=b for a). To show not surjective: provide b∈B with no a having f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof is an existence proof; constructing an explicit preimage or giving a formula in terms of b suffices. Be mindful of codomain: changing the codomain can change surjectivity status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving non-injectivity/non-surjectivity (negations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove injectivity: find distinct a,a' with f(a)=f(a'). To disprove surjectivity: show ∃b∈B ∀a∈A f(a)≠b (i.e., exhibit a codomain element with no preimage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are typical counterexample-based disproofs; the text emphasizes constructing explicit examples.
